title: Filter out null or empty employee names from the list.
shortTitle: Filter out null or empty employee names from the list

s1_definition.profdef: This is a data-cleansing `filter` whose predicate retains only elements with a usable name, rejecting both `null` references and empty or blank strings. The idiomatic check is `name != null && !name.trim().isEmpty()`, which survives only non-null, non-blank names.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is cleaning the staff list before printing. Some entries have no name at all (a blank slot) and some have just empty spaces. She throws those away and keeps only the real names. That cleanup is the filter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep only names that are not null and not blank by checking non-null first, then non-empty after trimming whitespace.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a data-cleansing `filter` whose predicate retains only elements with a usable name, rejecting both `null` references and empty or blank strings. The idiomatic check is `name != null && !name.trim().isEmpty()`, which survives only non-null, non-blank names.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is cleaning the staff list before printing. Some entries have no name at all (a blank slot) and some have just empty spaces. She throws those away and keeps only the real names. That cleanup is the filter.

**One line to remember:** Keep only names that are not null and not blank by checking non-null first, then non-empty after trimming whitespace.

sections.s2_technical:
There are two bad states to reject. The first is `null`, an absent reference, and calling any method on it throws a `NullPointerException`. The second is an empty or whitespace-only string like the empty string or a few spaces, which is technically a valid object but useless as a name.

The order of the checks is essential. You must test `name != null` first, then test the content, because Java short-circuits the AND and will not evaluate the second part if the first is false. If you reversed the order and called a method on a null name, you would crash. So the predicate is `name != null && !name.trim().isEmpty()`.

Calling `trim()` removes leading and trailing whitespace, so a name made only of spaces becomes the empty string and `isEmpty()` then returns true, which the NOT flips to false, rejecting it. On Java 11 and later you can use `isBlank()` directly, which treats whitespace-only as blank without an explicit trim, so `name != null && !name.isBlank()` is even cleaner.

A senior nuance: this is a classic place for a reusable utility predicate, because "has a real value" is checked all over a codebase. Many teams keep a `StringUtils.isNotBlank` helper (Apache Commons provides one) so the intent is named and consistent everywhere.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India imports employee records from an old legacy system, and the import is dirty: some rows have a null name because the field was never filled, and some have just blank spaces where a name should be. Before the data can be used for payroll or the printed directory it must be cleansed so that every remaining record has a real, usable name. This is exactly how a cleansing filter works — each name is checked for being non-null and non-blank, and only the clean records survive.

The code defines an `Employee` with name and id. A `DataCleansingService` exposes `withValidNames(List<Employee>)` using a null-then-blank predicate. The runnable `Main` feeds a dirty imported list including nulls and blanks and logs the clean records.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: E1 Rajesh, E2 null, E3 three spaces, E4 Priya, E5 empty string.

Step 1: The stream opens over five imported records.

Step 2: E1 enters. Name is not null, and after trim "Rajesh" is not empty, so both pass — kept.

Step 3: E2 enters. Name is null, so the first test fails and short-circuiting skips the trim call, avoiding a null pointer exception — dropped safely.

Step 4: E3 enters. Name is not null, but trimming three spaces yields the empty string, isEmpty is true, NOT true is false — dropped.

Step 5: E4 enters. Not null, "Priya" not empty — kept.

Step 6: E5 enters. Not null, but the empty string trimmed is still empty, so isEmpty is true — dropped.

Step 7: `collect` gathers E1 and E4.

```

Oct 30, 2026 11:15:06 AM com.bank.cleansing.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Clean record: E1:Rajesh
Oct 30, 2026 11:15:06 AM com.bank.cleansing.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Clean record: E4:Priya
Oct 30, 2026 11:15:06 AM com.bank.cleansing.Main lambda$main$1
INFO: Kept 2 of 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input (dirty import): [E1 Rajesh, E2 null, E3 "   ", E4 Priya, E5 ""]
    │
    ▼
  stream()
    │
    ▼
  filter(name != null && !name.trim().isEmpty())
    ├─ E1 "Rajesh" → notNull notBlank → PASS ─┐
    ├─ E2 null     → notNull (short-circuit)     DROP │
    ├─ E3 "   "    → notNull trim→"" empty       DROP │
    ├─ E4 "Priya"  → notNull notBlank → PASS ─┤
    └─ E5 ""       → notNull empty               DROP │
                                                   ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [E1 Rajesh, E4 Priya]
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Null/Blank Cleansing Filter ═══

  ┌─ Order matters ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ name != null  (FIRST) → short-circuit avoids NPE     │
  │ !name.trim().isEmpty() → rejects "" and "   "        │
  │ Java 11+: !name.isBlank() is equivalent and cleaner  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
  │        DataCleansingService          │uses│    Employee     │
  │ ──────────────────────────────────── │──▶│ ────────────── │
  │ + withValidNames(List): List         │   │ - name: String  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘   └────────────────┘

  Contract for withValidNames:
    Pre:  list non-null (elements may have null/blank names)
    Post: returns only records with a real, non-blank name
    Never throws on null name (guard-first design)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To cleanse a list of two bad states — null and blank — I filter with a predicate that first checks the name is not null and then checks it is not empty after trimming whitespace. The order is essential: the null check must come first, because Java short-circuits the AND and would otherwise call a method on a null reference and throw a null pointer exception. After confirming it is not null, I trim the whitespace and test that what remains is not the empty string, which rejects both a truly empty value and a value that is only spaces.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this came up when we imported employee records from a legacy system. The import was dirty — some rows had a null name because the field was never populated, and some had just blank spaces. Before the data could feed payroll or the printed directory it had to be cleansed so every surviving record had a real, usable name, so I streamed the import and kept only the valid ones.

A senior point I add is that on Java 11 and later I prefer the isBlank method, which treats a whitespace-only string as blank without an explicit trim, so the predicate becomes name not null and not blank, which is cleaner and expresses intent directly. Because "has a real value" is checked all over a codebase, I treat this as a reusable utility — teams often keep a named helper such as isNotBlank so the intent is consistent everywhere and the cleansing rule is defined in exactly one place rather than copied around.

keyPoints: Uses filter() with a Predicate<T> to select matching elements
Lazy operation — no processing until terminal operation
Can chain multiple filters or use complex Predicate with && ||
